description:
Borowa Palace is described as an 18th-century residence of the von Schwerin family, which owned it until 1945; sources differ on its origins, and one regional guide says it began as a 16th-century Renaissance building on a moated island that was rebuilt in the Baroque style in the 18th century. A tower and annexes were added at the turn of the 19th and 20th centuries.

In 1943 crates of valuable items from the Staatsarchiv Breslau and the Silesian Museum, along with private collections, began to be brought to the palace, one of the hiding places organised by Günther Grundmann; part of the collection was removed in December 1944, and much of the rest was dispersed, looted or destroyed after the war. After 1945 the palace housed Soviet troops, and from 1969 it passed to a state farm (PGR) with offices and common rooms; later it housed a school that operated until 2005.

In 2005 the municipality of Długołęka sold it; a private investor began a thorough restoration in 2007, completed on 5 February 2009, to turn it into a hotel and conference centre set in a landscape park.

faqs.question: How old is Borowa Palace?
faqs.answer: Sources differ: one describes it as an 18th-century von Schwerin palace, while a regional guide says it began as a 16th-century Renaissance building that was rebuilt in the Baroque style in the 18th century. A tower and annexes were added around 1900.

faqs.answer: Not on the rate we saw; breakfast is offered for about €9 extra.

hotel.room_location_note: Rooms are in Pałac Borowa Rezydencja, the palace hotel at Lipowa 34
hotel.how_to_stay:
**Getting there:** At Lipowa 34 in Borowa, in Długołęka Municipality near Wrocław, in Lower Silesia; Booking lists free private parking.

**Rooms & rates:** From approx. €66/night for a 25 m² Double Room with two twin beds, a garden view, a private bathroom and free Wi-Fi, on the non-refundable rate seen (pay online); about €5 in taxes is shown separately. A rate with free cancellation was around €73. Breakfast is not included (about €9 extra).

**On-site:** Free private parking and free Wi-Fi.

**Good to know:** Breakfast is charged separately. The palace was used as a state-farm office and a school after the Second World War and was restored in 2007–2009, so expect a historic building that has been remodelled several times.

**Combine with:** [More castle hotels in Poland](/castle-hotels/poland).
